sum: Shares in Singapore Telecommunications (Singtel) gained the most in three months after posting a 10 per cent rise in first-half underlying net profit on Friday, and raising its forecast for annual operating earnings from its core units.
Shares rose as much as three per cent in early trade, marking their biggest intraday gain since mid-August and outperforming the broader benchmark, which was down 0.4 per cent.
Southeast Asia's largest telecom operator said underlying net profit for the six months ended Sept 30 was $1.49 billion, up from $1.35 billion a year earlier.

Bolstered by the stellar first-half showing, Singtel now expects fiscal 2027 earnings before interest and tax for the operating company, excluding contributions from regional associates, to grow in the mid- to high-single digits, up from the previously forecast low- to mid-single-digit growth.

Operating revenue from Optus, Australia's second-largest telecommunications provider, which Singtel has owned since 2001, fell two per cent during the half-year, but stronger mobile performance and cost management translated into improved profitability.

Long a key earnings contributor for Singtel, Optus has faced a series of operational and reputational challenges in recent years, including cyber and network outages that sparked political and regulatory backlash.
Post-tax contributions from regional associates including India's Bharti Airtel, Thailand's Advanced Info Service (AIS) and Indonesia's Telkomsel rose nine per cent to $993 million.

Singapore's DBS warns of uncertain outlook as market volatility drives Q3 profit miss
sum: Singapore's largest bank, DBS Group, warned on Thursday of growing global uncertainty due to elevated energy prices, higher interest rates and geopolitical risks as market volatility pushed its earnings lower.

DBS, which is also Southeast Asia's biggest lender by assets, said July–September net profit fell 5 percent to S$2.81 billion (HK$17.26 billion) from a year earlier, mainly on a decline in markets trading income.
The result undershot the mean estimate of S$2.90 billion from four analysts, according to LSEG data, even though its wealth management division posted a strong performance.
The group's markets trading income sank 65 percent year-on-year to S$152 million for the quarter, which DBS attributed to "unfavourable equity market conditions".
The bank's net interest margin, a key profitability gauge, fell 9 basis points year-on-year to 1.87 percent.

The decline underscores how surging global bond yields, a rout in high-flying technology stocks last quarter and the ongoing Middle East conflict are beginning to bite into Singapore lenders' earnings after strong wealth management momentum cushioned their bottom lines in the first half.
Shares of DBS, which have risen 24 percent so far this year, fell more than 2 percent to S$69.27 in early trading.

DBS Group stock faces earnings test as trading income plunges
sum: DBS Group reported lower third-quarter profit after a sharp decline in markets trading income outweighed growth in lending, wealth management and customer fees. In its third-quarter trading update dated November 5, DBS said net profit for the three months ended September 30 fell 5 percent year on year to SGD 2.813 billion. Profit was also 9 percent below the second quarter.

Total income declined 1 percent from a year earlier to SGD 5.845 billion and fell 4 percent sequentially. The main drag was markets trading income, which dropped 65 percent year on year to SGD 152 million amid unfavourable market conditions. Compared with the second quarter, the decline was 68 percent.

DBS said net interest income rose 4 percent year on year to SGD 3.711 billion. Hedging and balance-sheet growth helped offset the impact of lower Singapore Overnight Rate Average levels. Net interest margin was 1.87 percent in the quarter.

Net fee income increased 6 percent to SGD 1.432 billion. Wealth management fees rose 9 percent to SGD 864 million, while assets under management reached a record SGD 544 billion after strong net new money inflows. Commercial-book other non-interest income rose 19 percent to SGD 685 million, supported mainly by treasury customer sales.

The broader nine-month picture remained stronger than the quarterly headline. Net profit for the first nine months rose 2 percent to a record SGD 8.822 billion, while total income increased 2 percent to SGD 17.886 billion. Return on equity was 17.0 percent, and the non-performing-loan ratio improved to 0.9 percent at the end of September.

For 2027, DBS expects total income growth in the mid-single-digit range. The outlook assumes two further US Federal Reserve rate increases by the end of next year, average SORA of about 1.6 percent and a stronger Singapore dollar. The bank expects loan and deposit growth to support net interest income, while structural expansion in wealth management should continue.

Chief executive Tan Su Shan said the global outlook had become more uncertain because of elevated energy prices, tighter financial conditions and geopolitical risks. She said DBS would remain nimble while managing risks, with capital, liquidity and general allowance buffers providing resilience.

DBS Group stock faces earnings test after third-quarter miss
sum: DBS Group reported a weaker third quarter on November 5, as a sharp decline in markets trading income outweighed continued growth in wealth management and fee income. CNA reported that net profit for the July-to-September period fell 5 percent year on year to S$2.81 billion, below the S$2.90 billion average forecast from four analysts surveyed by LSEG.

The main drag came from markets trading income, which plunged 65 percent from a year earlier to S$152 million. DBS attributed the decline to unfavourable equity market conditions, while its net interest margin narrowed by nine basis points to 1.87 percent.

The result also shows that the bank's customer franchises continued to provide support. Wealth management fees increased 9 percent year on year to S$864 million, and net fee income rose 6 percent to S$1.43 billion. Those gains were not enough to offset the trading setback, leaving investors to weigh the durability of customer-led growth against more volatile markets revenue.

DBS expects total income to rise in the mid-single-digit range in 2027. Management said structural growth in wealth management should continue, while Chief Executive Tan Su Shan cautioned that the global outlook had become more uncertain because of market and geopolitical risks.

For investors, the earnings mix is important. The quarter showed that lending profitability and wealth-related fees can cushion weaker capital-markets activity, but it also highlighted the sensitivity of quarterly earnings to trading conditions. The next results will indicate whether fee growth and balance-sheet expansion can keep offsetting pressure on markets income and margins.

items.t: Banco Do Brasil Shares Slid Even Though Sales Rose
sum: Brazil's state controlled lender just reported Q2 2026 results showing revenue at R$21,915.374m and net income at R$2,397.643m, with net margin at 10.9% versus 12.7% a year earlier. Holding Banco do Brasil over the past year would have meant a 22.5% loss, including dividends. If you had bought on 6 November 2025, that headline number is the experience to explain. The open question now is whether current profitability justifies renewed optimism about its digital and agribusiness initiatives.
If the move has made Banco do Brasil harder to judge, start where the gap is still open and scan 217 high quality undervalued stocks.
The shares cost R$22.86 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at Banco do Brasil then had to choose between two very different scripts.

The bullish story saw digital acceleration and a rising middle class reshaping the bank, with a Fair Value of R$39, a price that assumed revenue could grow 12.7% a year and eSocial driven payroll lending would scale rapidly.
The cautious view argued fintech rivalry and regulation might bite harder, with a Fair Value of R$20 based on 8.9% revenue growth and persistent asset quality pressure in agribusiness and MSMEs.

The clearest new fact is that Banco do Brasil's Q2 2026 revenue sat at R$21,915.374m versus R$21,873.133m a year earlier. Net income moved from R$2,782.083m to R$2,397.643m and net margin slipped from 12.7% to 10.9%. That pattern of slightly higher sales but thinner profitability leaned toward the cautious script that worried about pressure on earnings quality.

The useful takeaway for any bank you follow is simple. When a bullish pitch hangs on improving efficiency and profitability, check whether net income and net margin move in the same direction as revenue in later results, not just whether the top line holds steady.

sum: In this column, ST’s business correspondents unpack the latest developments in Singapore and global markets during the week – and explain what they mean for investors.

SINGAPORE – Singapore’s three major banks saw their share prices drop this week. This followed DBS and UOB reporting lower-than-expected earnings and net interest margins for the third quarter ending Sept 30.

DBS closed on Nov 6 at $69.72, down 3.78% from Nov 2 when it opened at $72.46, as net profit for the quarter missed estimates and fell 5% to $2.81 billion due to lower market trading income amid unfavourable equity market conditions.

The group’s markets trading income sank 65% year on year to $152 million for the quarter because of weaker Asian asset performance, dislocated equity market volatility, rising interest rates towards the end of the third quarter, and a drop in volume.

The bank announced on Nov 5 that its chairman Peter Seah will retire at the end of 2026 after 16 years at the helm, with board member Anthony Lim taking over from Jan 1, 2027. Seah will be appointed senior adviser for a year.
UOB shares fell 10.27% over the week, closing at $36.83 from the week’s high of $41.10 on Nov 2.
The bank’s third-quarter net profit jumped 182% to $1.25 billion from a year earlier, on the back of strong growth in wealth, cards and loan-related activities.

Singapore Banks Face Slower Growth in 2027 as Deposit Competition Bites
sum: Analysts expect Singapore’s banks to face slower growth in 2027 as deposit competition squeezes margins and wealth fees weaken. The outlook follows mixed third-quarter results: OCBC beat estimates, while DBS and UOB fell short. Analysts say the banks remain on different footing.

Singapore’s three largest banks may see slower growth in 2027 as deposit competition and weaker wealth fees pressure earnings, analysts said after mixed third-quarter results. The outlook matters to investors tracking the banks’ performance as DBS and UOB missed analysts’ expectations, while OCBC beat them.
“The boom years did a lot of the work for Singapore’s banks,” said Eric Xiao, head of sales in Asia for CMC Markets. “In 2027, they’ll have to do it themselves.”

Xiao said DBS took in a record S$15 billion (US$11.7 billion) of net new money in the third quarter, but wealth fees fell 6 per cent as clients traded less. He said monetizing the wealth boom appeared more difficult than expected.

Higher interest rates could eventually help banks, Xiao said, but margins may initially come under pressure because deposit rates tend to rise faster than loan rates. He did not expect a “down year” for the banks despite the tougher conditions.

Ritesh Ganeriwal, group head of investment and advisory at Syfe, said the banks’ core business held up in the third quarter, but “the problem is that interest rates are no longer doing the heavy lifting”.

Singapore rates have remained low even as US rates rise, while banks compete harder for deposits, Ganeriwal said. He expects slower growth in 2027, driven by loans and wealth fees, rather than a downturn.

sum: DBS Group is heading into a closely watched third-quarter earnings release on Thursday, November 5, 2026. A MarketWatch earnings preview published on November 2 said analysts expect profit to edge lower while total income increases.

A consensus of nine analysts polled by Visible Alpha points to third-quarter net profit of SGD 2.93 billion, down 0.7 percent from the year-earlier period. Six analysts expect total income to rise 2.7 percent to SGD 6.09 billion.

The forecast suggests that revenue growth may not fully offset pressure on the bottom line. Jefferies analysts cited normalizing fees and weaker market-related income as potential offsets to resilient non-interest income. Maybank Securities analyst Thilan Wickramasinghe said softer equity markets and higher bond yields may have weighed on trading income.

Investors are expected to focus on DBS's wealth management business, which has supported earnings in recent quarters. The bank is targeting assets under management of SGD 1 trillion in the segment, making client flows and recurring fee generation important indicators for the results and the outlook.

The earnings release should also clarify whether loan growth and interest-sensitive income can cushion pressure on margins. Credit costs, capital returns and cost control will be relevant for assessing the durability of the bank's profitability as interest-rate conditions evolve.

Management's comments on the 2026 and 2027 outlook are likely to receive close attention. The market will be looking for indications on net interest income, wealth fees, trading income and the pace at which profitability can adjust to changing rates.

DBS Stock Drops 0.91% on Friday, Testing Support Level
sum: On October 30, 2026: price 73.13 SGD, trend downtrend, RSI 33.1, support 73.13, resistance 78.56. technical analysis of dbs stock. DBS Stock Drops — full…

DBS Group closed at S$73.13 on Friday, October 30, 2026, down 0.91% for the session and 1.76% over five days. The stock is close to its three-month low of S$72.50 while its decline continues, putting the focus on whether selling pressure eases near the bottom of the recent range. The latest session’s volume was 1.3 times its 20-day average, while on-balance volume fell—a sign that heavier trading has not yet confirmed a shift in demand.

The short-term structure remains weak. DBS traded below its 20-day moving average of S$74.66, which itself fell 1.29% over five days, and below its 50-day average of S$76.23. No new moving-average crossover was reported. The lack of a fresh crossover does not alter the underlying message: price and the shorter-term average remain beneath the longer-term reference, while the short-term average is declining.

The price sat at the bottom of its 20-trading-day range, between support at S$73.13 and resistance at S$78.56. The three-month low of S$72.50 is nearby, but proximity to a low is not, by itself, evidence of a reversal. The session’s close also matches the stated 20-day support level, making the next response around this zone especially relevant.
As shown in the chart, price is positioned below both moving averages and near the lower part of the recent range.

The indicators show weakness, but not a uniform signal of an established rebound. The RSI is 33.1, classified as neutral in the supplied data; it is close to the lower end of the scale, but does not independently confirm a turn. The Stochastic is oversold, with %K at 14.5 and %D at 34.1. That can occur when selling has been persistent; an oversold reading is not a timing signal unless price and momentum begin to recover.

The MACD remains negative: at -0.766, it is below its -0.708 signal line, and its histogram is -0.058. This points to negative momentum rather than a confirmed bullish divergence. Taken together, the readings suggest the stock may be stretched near support, while the broader momentum picture still leans downward.

sum: (Oct 8): Major banks in Southeast Asia declined more than 1% on Thursday, with the region's top lender, DBS Group, dragging Singapore stocks more than 3% lower as rising bond yields brought into focus risks to bank earnings growth and funding costs.
The MSCI EM Asia equities index declined 1.8% in its worst day since early September, largely weighed down by a 2.6% drop in South Korea's Kospi.

In Singapore, the FTSE Straits Times index shed as much as 3.2% to hit its lowest since mid-July, with DBS dipping 5.2% to mark its steepest daily loss since April last year. Smaller rivals OCBC and UOB fell nearly 5% each. Together, the three banks account for more than half of Singapore's main index, and make up more than a third of the MSCI Asean equity gauge, which marked its worst daily drop since early March.

JPMorgan and Citi raised concerns over Asean banks' earnings outlook, citing surging long-dated bond yields, higher funding costs and the normalisation of exceptional first-half wealth-related income.

"A combination of higher rates, AQ (asset quality) risks, funding tightness and capital-market-related revenue risks should impact quite a few bank stocks going into 3Q results," JPMorgan analysts led by Harsh Wardhan Modi wrote.
They recommend trimming exposure to all three major Singapore banks.
After a strong run in bank shares, investors may have become more sensitive to earnings risks and negative catalysts, said James Ooi, market strategist at Tiger Brokers.

sum: DBS reported a 1% increase in profit and maintained its 1Q26 ordinary dividend of S$0.66, alongside a S$0.15 capital return, bringing total dividends to S$0.81.
DBS has announced its earnings for first quarter of 2026. Key highlights include:
- 1Q 2026 pre-tax profit: SGD 3.51 billion (+2% year-over-year)
- 1Q 2026 net profit: SGD 2.93 billion (+1% year-over-year), a record start to the year
- Total income: SGD 5.95 billion, a new high (+1% year-over-year, +12% quarter-on-quarter)
#1 - Total income at record high despite continued rate headwinds

1Q26 net profit rose 1% year-on-year to S$2.93 billion as record fee income, stronger treasury customer sales and higher markets trading income more than offset the impact of lower interest rates and a stronger Singapore dollar.

DBS shares rally to new high of $55.54 as Q3 earnings beat expectations
sum: SINGAPORE - Shares of DBS surged past $55 for the first time on Nov 6 after Singapore’s largest bank posted a smaller-than-expected drop in third-quarter earnings as lower interest rates squeeze margins.

The stock opened at $53.90, crossed the $55 mark at 9.15am and continued to rise throughout the day. At the close of trading, DBS was up 3.8 per cent or $2.04 to $55.54, after 13.1 million shares changed hands.

The bank’s net profit for the three months to Sept 30 dipped 2 per cent to $2.95 billion, from $3.03 billion in the year-ago period, but beat the $2.79 billion forecast by analysts in a Bloomberg poll.
The bank declared an interim one-tier dividend of 60 cents and a one-tier capital return dividend of 15 cents for each ordinary share.
This brings the quarter’s total dividend payout to 75 cents per share, compared with the 54 cents in the year-ago period.
DBS said commercial book net interest income in the quarter fell 6 per cent to $3.56 billion as lower rates were mitigated by hedging and deposit growth.
Commercial book net interest margin declined 43 basis points to 2.4 per cent, from 2.83 per cent in the year-ago period.

DBS hits new record of $55.55 with higher dividend commitment
sum: DBS Group Holdings' share price hit a new record of $55.55 after it reported better-than-expected 3QFY2025 earnings. A commitment to increase its already generous dividend payout for the coming FY2026 sent the bank's market cap above $157 billion.

In the coming year, DBS plans to increase its quarterly ordinary dividend payout by 6 cents to 66 cents, which means an additional 24 cents for FY2026. In addition, there's 15 cents per share to be paid in capital return dividend, which has been committed up to FY2027, which works out to 81 cents per quarter.
"We will get it approved at the AGM in March 2026, and then it will actually flow through," says CFO Chng Sok Hui at the bank's results briefing.
Based on DBS's current full-year dividend of $3, comprising 60 cents ordinary dividend and 15 cents capital return per quarter, the dividend yield works out at 5.4%.
"We've always said that we had $8 billion of excess stock of capital to return. We remain committed to returning that," says CEO Tan Su Shan at the same briefing.
Of this $8 billion, $3 billion has been allocated to share buybacks and thus far, 12% of that amount spent.
"Our philosophy is to buy when the market is bad," says Tan.
